record.original_question: Prove that the Riemann zeta function zeta(s) has at least one nontrivial zero rho = beta + i gamma whose positive imaginary part gamma is irrational.

evidence.quote: Problem 1: Prove that ζ(s) has at least one(!) irrational ordinate.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, defined for $\Re(s) > 1$ by $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ and extended by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with a single simple pole at $s = 1$. A nontrivial zero of $\zeta$ is a zero $\rho = \beta + i\gamma$ with $0 < \beta < 1$. Prove that there exists at least one nontrivial zero $\rho = \beta + i\gamma$ of $\zeta(s)$ whose imaginary part $\gamma > 0$ is an irrational number.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of showing that even a single nontrivial zero of $\zeta(s)$ has irrational imaginary part appears to be open. Although numerical evidence strongly suggests all computed ordinates are irrational (indeed believed to be transcendental and linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$), no proof is known that establishes irrationality for any specific ordinate or for the existence of one.

status_evidence.title: Riemann zeta function - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Conjectures regarding the arithmetic nature of zeta zero ordinates remain unproven.
status_evidence.claim: No proof is known that any nontrivial zero of zeta has irrational imaginary part.

status_evidence.title: Two arguments that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are irrational
status_evidence.snippet: Heuristic arguments concerning the irrationality of ordinates of nontrivial zeros.
status_evidence.claim: The irrationality of zeta zero ordinates is treated as a conjecture, not a theorem.
